```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)
```

`gof` checks fitted models using cumulative residual processes. A process
adds residuals in the order of a covariate or fitted prediction. Sustained
departures can reveal a mean structure that the fitted model has missed.
The package compares the observed process with simulated null processes
that account for coefficient estimation.

This guide starts with a linear model, then covers the evaluation grid,
missing observations, grouped binomial responses, weights and offsets.
The [statistical details vignette](statistical-details.html) explains the
method, model support and reproducibility assumptions.

## Fit, diagnose and inspect

The following data have a curved mean relationship. We deliberately fit a
straight line so that the diagnostic has a useful question to investigate.

```{r linear-model}
library(gof)

set.seed(101)
d <- data.frame(x = runif(180, -2, 2))
d$y <- 1 + 0.7 * d$x + 0.6 * d$x^2 + rnorm(nrow(d))
fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = d)

set.seed(102)
diagnostic <- fit |>
  cumres(variable = "x", R = 199, plots = 12)

diagnostic |> summary()
```

The fitted model is the first argument to `cumres()`, so the base R pipe
`|>` works directly. The same call can be written as
`cumres(fit, variable = "x", R = 199, plots = 12)`.

```{r linear-plot}
diagnostic |> plot()
```

The thick line is the observed cumulative residual process. The other
lines are simulated processes under the fitted null model. They help
visualize the scale and shape of departures; the collection of plotted
lines is not a simultaneous confidence band.

For a table suitable for filtering, reporting or combining with other
results, use the data frame method:

```{r result-table}
diagnostic |> as.data.frame()
```

The table has an explicit ordering-variable column and one row for each
Sup or L2 test. The existing `coef(diagnostic)` method remains available
as a compact table of p-values; its name does not mean that the entries
are the fitted model's regression coefficients. Those are `coef(fit)`.

## What the tests mean

The Sup statistic measures the largest absolute departure of the process.
The L2 statistic combines departures over the selected ordering grid.
A small p-value is evidence against the fitted mean structure in the
direction examined by that process. It does not identify a unique repair.
Compare plausible model changes with the scientific question and the
observed data; repeatedly trying models until a p-value becomes large is
not an independent validation exercise.

A large p-value does not establish that every part of the model is
correct. These default `cumres()` calls provide marginal model checks, and
several ordering variables or tests produce several comparisons. Use
`cumres_joint()` for a prespecified ordering family under its documented
joint null; the marginal calls do not enable that inference automatically.

`R` is the number of null simulations used for the p-values. The examples
use small values to keep the guide quick to run. Use more simulations when
Monte Carlo uncertainty matters to a reported conclusion, and record the
seed and options. `plots` controls how many simulated curves are retained
for inspection; it is not a confidence level.

## The grid cap does not discard observations

For the lm/glm, SEM and default methods, `subset.max` limits the number of
distinct ordering values at which each process is evaluated. It does not
reduce the number of fitted observations. Its default is 500; use `Inf` or
`NULL` to evaluate every distinct value. The ordinal method uses its full
distinct-value grid and does not expose this option.

```{r evaluation-grid}
set.seed(103)
many <- data.frame(x = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 650))
many$y <- 1 + 0.5 * many$x + rnorm(nrow(many))
many_fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = many)

set.seed(104)
reduced_grid <- cumres(many_fit, variable = "x", subset.max = 75,
                       R = 99, plots = 0)
set.seed(104)
full_grid <- cumres(many_fit, variable = "x", subset.max = Inf,
                    R = 99, plots = 0)

data.frame(
  grid = c("at most 75 points", "all distinct values"),
  fitted_rows = c(reduced_grid$nobs, full_grid$nobs),
  evaluation_points = c(length(reduced_grid$x[[1]]),
                        length(full_grid$x[[1]]))
)
```

Changing the grid changes the evaluated approximation to the process, so
p-values need not be identical. Every observation tied at an ordering
value enters together. The package does not add numerical jitter or take
partial sums inside a tie group.

## Use the same observations as the fit

The lm/glm adapter follows the observations used by the fitted model,
including its missing-data exclusions. For example:

```{r missing-observations}
incomplete <- d
incomplete$y[c(4, 17)] <- NA_real_
incomplete_fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = incomplete, na.action = na.exclude)

set.seed(105)
incomplete_diagnostic <- cumres(incomplete_fit, variable = "x",
                               R = 99, plots = 0)
c(input_rows = nrow(incomplete), fitted_rows = nobs(incomplete_fit),
  diagnostic_rows = incomplete_diagnostic$nobs)
```

For an additional ordering covariate supplied through `data`, retain the
original row names so that it can be aligned to the fitted rows, or supply
the values already in fitted-row order. Additional orderings must also be
scientifically appropriate: their indicators must have centered residuals
under the null model. Being a finite numeric column alone does not prove
that property.

## Grouped binomial data and trial counts

Grouped binomial diagnostics retain the fitted coefficients and expand
success/failure contributions into individual Bernoulli trials without
refitting the model. Equal group sizes, subsets and offsets do not require
reconstructing the original fitting call.

```{r grouped-binomial}
set.seed(106)
groups <- data.frame(x = seq(-1.5, 1.5, length.out = 120), trials = 10L)
groups$known_log_odds <- rep(c(-0.3, 0.3), length.out = nrow(groups))
groups$successes <- rbinom(nrow(groups), groups$trials,
                           plogis(-0.4 + 0.8 * groups$x + groups$known_log_odds))
groups$failures <- groups$trials - groups$successes
grouped_fit <- glm(cbind(successes, failures) ~ x + offset(known_log_odds),
                   data = groups, family = binomial())

set.seed(107)
grouped_diagnostic <- grouped_fit |>
  cumres(variable = "x", R = 99, plots = 0)
c(fitted_groups = grouped_diagnostic$nobs,
  residual_trials = grouped_diagnostic$n)
grouped_diagnostic |> as.data.frame()
```

The known log-odds adjustment is retained as an offset. The equivalent
proportion syntax is
`glm(successes / trials ~ x + offset(known_log_odds), weights = trials,
family = binomial(), data = groups)`.
Responses and weights must reconstruct nonnegative integer successes and
failures within floating-point roundoff. A proportion with an unknown
trial count does not provide enough information for this expansion.

## Precision weights and exposure offsets

For normal and Poisson models, prior weights describe the precision of
independent response means. They are not treated as repeated observations.
Zero-weight fitted rows are excluded from the diagnostic.

```{r precision-weights}
set.seed(108)
weighted <- data.frame(x = runif(180, -1, 1))
weighted$precision <- 1 + 3 * (weighted$x + 1)^2
weighted$y <- 1 + 0.5 * weighted$x +
  rnorm(nrow(weighted), sd = 1 / sqrt(weighted$precision))
weighted_fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = weighted, weights = precision)

set.seed(109)
weighted_fit |> cumres(variable = "x", R = 99, plots = 0) |> as.data.frame()
```

For a Poisson rate model, include the exposure in the fitted model's
offset. The diagnostic uses that full fitted linear predictor.

```{r poisson-offset}
set.seed(110)
rates <- data.frame(x = runif(160, -1, 1), exposure = runif(160, 0.5, 4))
rates$events <- rpois(nrow(rates),
                      rates$exposure * exp(-0.5 + 0.7 * rates$x))
rate_fit <- glm(events ~ x + offset(log(exposure)),
                data = rates, family = poisson())

set.seed(111)
rate_fit |> cumres(variable = "x", R = 99, plots = 0) |> as.data.frame()
```

## Find help and keep a reproducible record

`?cumres` introduces the generic and supported methods. For model-specific
arguments and restrictions, use `?cumres.glm`, `?cumres.lvmfit` or
`?cumres.ordreg`. Plot options are described in `?plot.cumres`.

Record the input data, fitted model, random seed, diagnostic options and
package versions with a reported analysis. The next vignette gives a
compact reproducibility record and examples for SEMs, ordinal models and
the custom residual interface.
